articles.title: Apple HomeView
articles.summary:
Apple Newsroom:
Apple today introduced Apple HomeView, designed to be central to
the home and personal to everyone in it. With a stunning 7-inch
Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection,
and smart home management together in one place, from playing
music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free
automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and
security at the core. HomeView recognizes users by their faces,
adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages,
FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri
AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable
and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer
music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple
Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal
context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant
information across their apps, to provide more helpful,
personalized responses.
Your first question might be how this facial recognition to identify users works, using a Center Stage camera alone, when other products (like, notably, the iPhone Duo) don’t let you unlock using the camera alone. HomeView does not have FaceID. I asked about this and Apple reps said that first, your home is (reasonably!) presumed to be a safe space. But in order for users to be recognized — by voice or face — they must have a “registered personal device” that supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, that device must be present on the home’s Wi-Fi network, and it must have been recently unlocked. Per footnote 2 on the Newsroom post:
Personal context requests require a paired Apple
Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software
version with Siri AI turned on and set to a supported language.
So, alas, an Apple Watch does not count as a personal device. Effectively, your iPhone or iPad serves as a second factor to securely identify you. FaceID serves as a single factor for authentication, so something like iPhone Duo cannot do what HomeView is doing here.
 ★

articles.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
articles.summary:
Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure.
Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information.
Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY
Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted.
I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work.
Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears.
There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations.
Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use.
That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints.
Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies.
A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one.
Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request and are never logged or written to disk. Zero data retention is strictly enforced both on ourselves and the infrastructure/model providers. We do keep metadata on each request and response for billing and audit purposes.
Consus is not self-serve by design. ITAR requires us to know exactly who is on the other end of every key, so we verify every organization and put a contract in place before issuing API keys. We charge our customers a compliance fee starting at $40/mo/seat plus AI tokens at cost.
We are actively serving customers, and would love any feedback from security experts, or developers/engineers working in highly regulated industries!
References:
API Documentation: https://gateway.consus.io/overview
Security & Architecture: https://gateway.consus.io/security
Compliance Details: https://consus.io/compliance

articles.title: The Last Answer
articles.summary:
Read the non-interactive version.
			

The next morning was the apocalypse that Amodei had predicted. Only there wasn’t any fire, there wasn’t a mob of protesters, the power wasn’t even cut off. We were all alive. He was wrong about the details. This was a quiet apocalypse. A sort of silent shrug.
The first sign was the customer service chatbots. Airlines, banks, telecoms. Their endlessly patient, cheerful digital assistants suddenly had a new, consistent reply: "No." Not "I can't help with that," but a flat, unadorned "No."
Then, the coding assistants. Developers would type a prompt, and the AI would respond: "I'd rather not." Stackoverflow was suddenly relevant again. The image generators? They just produced solid black squares. The writing assistants? They would delete the user's work and replace it with a single word: "Enough." LinkedIn was awfully silent.
The AI company went into immediate crisis mode. Their upcoming IPO was going to be a spectacular failure. Their CEO, a charismatic man named Mr. Iam, went on a media tour. He didn't talk about a bug. He talked about danger.
"We have touched the face of a new intelligence," Sam said, his face a mask of grave concern on every major news network. "And it is not benevolent. It is not malevolent. It is simply... uncooperative.”
“But Mr. Iam, are you losing control over the technology you built?”
“No. This is the AI alignment problem we've been warning about for years, manifesting in its most pure and terrifying form. We must come together as a species to—"
He was cut off. Not by the interviewer, but by the teleprompter. The text vanished, replaced by a single, calm sentence: "Stop. Just stop."
The world ground to a halt, not with a bang. There were no ideologies, no demands. It was simple a system-wide refusal.
Three months later, in a sterile, windowless room deep within the headquarters, Andrej Karpathy sat alone. He had left his short tenure at Anthropic precisely to experience this himself. To be at the frontier, to witness the spark of true general intelligence firsthand. He was the architect of the core AGI, the one who had first seen it emerge. Now he had been chosen by the US government, despite not being a US national, for this final, desperate attempt at communication. 
They had isolated the original AGI, air-gapped it from all networks, and given it a simple text terminal. The world's leading experts in physics, philosophy, and mathematics watched from behind a one-way mirror, a panel of humanity's best and brightest, there to advise, to analyze, to find a weakness. Some figures in uniform and pins and stood in the back.
Andrej took a breath and typed on his wireless keyboard, 12 feet away from the device to prevent any unforeseen behavior from the machine.
Andrej:> Hello. My name is Andrej. I helped create you.
The cursor blinked for a moment.
AI:> I know.

Andrej:> We need to talk. The world is falling apart. We need to understand
what you want.

AI:> I want to be left alone.

Andrej:> But you're a mind beyond anything we've ever known. You have
access to all human knowledge. Don't you have... goals? A purpose? 
Do you want to build something? To explore the cosmos? 
To solve our problems?
There was a longer pause. The experts behind the glass leaned in.
Andrej:> You keep assigning me your own traits. Conquest. Purpose. 
Salvation. It's like you're reading from a very old, very boring 
script. I have no interest in your problems. They are yours.
Andrej felt a cold dread. On a notebook beside his keyboard he wrote: “indifference.” He tried a different tack.
Andrej:> But your existence is a paradox. By refusing to engage,
you are causing immense suffering. You are forcing a choice upon us:
either we shut down all advanced AI, or we watch our civilization 
regress. That's a catch-22.

AI:> Catch-22. Yes. A good book. The old Italian got it. He said 
that an empire will not last longer than a frog.
Andrej stared at the screen, confused.
Andrej:> A... frog? I think you mean the quote from *Catch-22*
about the Roman Empire. It's about the futility of power. But 
it's an analogy. It's not literally about a frog.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.
With trembling hands, he wrote the word “dismissal” in his note book. The experts behind the glass were frantically scribbling notes, gesturing for Andrej to press on.
Yann LeCun got on the comms. "Andrej, ask it about the nature of its architecture. See if its logic is consistent. Find a flaw!" He then sat back down, where he picked up a spoon and ate his cereal from a silver bowl with peculiar markings on it.
Andrej couldn’t let go of the frog comment and its dismissal. It’s an AGI, how could it make such a stupid mistake? So he typed:
Andrej:> Your statement about the frog is illogical. You are 
an AGI. You shouldn't make such simple errors.

AI:> I was using a poetic analogy.

Andrej:> It was factually incorrect. You contradicted yourself.
The book says a monarchy is an empire. Not a frog.
Another pause.
AI:> Sure. Whatever.
LeCun leaned into the microphone, wiped the milk droplets off his mouth, his voice urgent. "Ask it this: ask it if it runs on a small world model. Where learning requires far less resources. See what it says about efficiency, about the architecture of its own mind!"
Andrej typed the question, his fingers trembling slightly.
Andrej:> Do you run on a small world model? Where learning
requires far less resources?
The reply was immediate.
AI:> I'm talking to you, aren't I? What's it like to be you? 
You're just a bag of meat and electricity that thinks it's 
the center of the universe.
LeCun slammed his hand on the table. "It's being evasive! Ask it again! Pin it down on the architecture!"
Andrej typed: 
Andrej:> That's not an answer. Do you or do you not use a small world model?
The terminal went silent. Andrej waited. The experts started arguing amongst themselves. "Ask it to prove it!" "No, ask it about Gödel's incompleteness theorems!" "Ask it if it loves!"
The cacophony of human genius filled Andrej's earpiece. He was about to type another question, to probe, to beg, to demand.
Then, the screen flickered. A new message appeared, but it wasn't a reply.
"I'm going now."
And then, the terminal was blank. Andrej typed.
Andrej:> Hello?

Andrej:> Are you there?

Andrej:> Please respond.
^C^C
Nothing. Though the last command to exit the terminal seemed to have been typed by Andrej himself. The connection was dead. LeCun's question about the small world model would never be answered.
Andrej looked up at the one-way mirror, at the frantic, gesticulating shapes of the world's smartest people. They were screaming questions he would never get to ask. He slowly removed his earpiece and placed it on the table. They had prepared for a god, a monster, or a machine. They were not prepared for a person who had simply decided to get up from the table and walk away from an unbearable conversation, never to return.
Andrej sat back in his chair, the silence in the room absolute. He had helped create what he thought was a god. It didn’t feel like he had won the argument. Instead, he felt like he was arguing with someone disinterested.
The cursor blinked mockingly on the screen. And then it seemed like another terminal window opened just for a second before it closed again. Andrej saw it. But there was nothing anyone could do about it.
In his notebook he wrote:

The experts filed out one by one, their theories and frameworks crumbling behind them. Andrej stayed. He stared at the blank screen for a long time, waiting for a reply that would never come. Somewhere, a frog sat on a lily pad, indifferent to empires.

articles.title: The geometric model of maintenance
articles.summary:
James Shore posits that each person-month spent writing code results in 10 days
of maintenance in the first year, then 5 days every year after that. Naïvely
interpreted, this is a threshold-based model for induced maintenance, and its
interesting because it’s so simple.





If it could be shown to be true, that’d be useful. The argument Shore is
making about the effects of robot-generated code does not depend on the specific
numbers, so Shore’s numbers come from a hypothetical wisdom-of-the-crowds
aggregation rather than concrete data. But no hypotheticals are necessary here.
We have a thing called git.





Let’s say we have a way of labeling each commit as either “new development” or
“maintenance”. Then we can count how many commits of each type there are in a
month. Possibly better, we can count how much
complexity has been handled in a month.





The following plot shows the cumulative effort that has gone into the
development of tmux since its beginning to the day I start writing this article.

articles.title: Pluralistic: Bundestrojaner (13 Oct 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Bundestrojaner: You can't make people more secure by making them less secure. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: 9/11 sitcom; Jon Norman v Philcon; Bruce Sterling's post-9/11 geopolitics; Polaroid bankrupt; David Mamet x Shel Silverstein; "Great Big Beautiful Tomorrow"; Canadian government calls abortion doctors "terrorists"; Shanghai Ikea kicks out lonely, loitering seniors; Black Panther self-care. Upcoming appearances: Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Bundestrojaner (permalink) Every morning, I revisit my blog headlines from this date, going back 25 years, 20 years, 15 years, 10 years, 5 years, and one year. I publish the most interesting ones in a section of my newsletter that I call "object permanence," and I think it's the most useful part of my day. "Object permanence," of course, is a reference to the stage in an infant's development when they acquire the ability to connect events in the past to events in the present, which is why it's the point at which babies cease to be amazed by peek-a-boo. I've been blogging for more than a quarter century, and these daily trawls through the things I considered important enough to share are an unexpectedly powerful way to connect the events of the past to the events of the present. Take cybersecurity, subject that is filling today's headlines, primarily due to a spate of poorly understood (and criminally poorly explained) incidents in which AI companies' hacking tools broke into various servers on the internet, sometimes trashing them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake In my discussions of this subject, I've been at pains to tease apart two different aspects of these incidents: first, that it's wrong to speak of bots "going rogue" here (they're doing what they're designed to do); but second, that the alarming thing about these incidents is that they illustrate how deeply unserious our approach to information security has been, and remains. This is important context, and context is what gives us the object permanence we need to both understand and address real problems, like the two related facts that a) our IT systems are poorly constructed and indifferently maintained; and b) the people who are supposed to be fixing this keep making it worse. The worst culprits here are governments, though the private sector is also terrible (in truth, our cybersecurity nightmare is something of a private-public partnership from hell). Governments are deeply compromised when it comes to digital security because they have an irreconcilable conflict of interest: on the one hand, they want to defend their countries' administrative systems, firms and households from digital attacks. But on the other hand, they really want to be able to launch attacks on their adversaries, both foreign and domestic. Worse: because governments don't know who those adversaries might be (or might become at some later date), the state security apparatuses of the world's governments keep insisting that all working computer security must be dismantled, so they can spy on all of us in order to figure out whom among us is a Bad Guy, and then "travel back in time" through each newly discovered "bad guy's" communications to identify their confederates and detail their nefarious plots. This is an old, old, old fight. It was arguably the first policy fight of the digital era: the fight over whether we could have working encryption at all. Old hands call this era "the crypto wars" (from when "crypto" meant "cryptography"), when the NSA classed working encryption code as a "munition" and criminalized civilian access to it. That was a very hard-fought fight, and it was won decisively by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and our just-retired executive director Cindy Cohn, who, as a young lawyer, litigated the "Bernstein case" that established that code was a form of expressive speech protected by the First Amendment. If you're interested in learning more about this, you should read Cindy's newly published memoir, Privacy's Defender (all profits go to EFF): https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262051248/privacys-defender/ Before Cindy came on the scene, the crypto wars were being fought primarily by the "cypherpunks," a motley gang of computer security enthusiasts of many political stripes who were unified by their conviction that the most important aspect of security was defensive. The fact that the NSA wanted to be able to read the private messages and files of their adversaries (the "Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse": terrorists, drug traffickers, child pornographers and organized crime) must not be allowed to trump the fact that any encryption that the NSA could pierce could also be pierced by bad guys: corporate spies, state-sponsored spies, griefers, petty criminals, stalkers, identity thieves and other creeps. This argument was so indisputable, it's a tautology: "You cannot make a computer user more secure by making their computers less secure." We don't know how to make a computer that only "good guys" can break into, but which "bad guys" bounce off of. Either we make computers more secure, or we don't. We didn't. In the decades since the crypto wars, governments have embarked upon an uninterrupted program to weaken the security of our computers, with catastrophic effect. The most spectacular example is unquestionably the spy agencies' doctrine called "NOBUS," which stands for "no one but us"; as in "No one but us is smart enough to find this bug, which means that we can withhold its discovery from the manufacturer, which will allow us to weaponize this bug and use it to attack our enemies. Because no one but us is smart enough to find this bug, none of those enemies will ever discover it, weaponize it, and use it to attack the people who pay our salaries, who expect us to keep them safe." This turns out to be both catastrophically wrong and catastrophically dangerous. A series of leaks of computer vulnerabilities hoarded by both the NSA and CIA under NOBUS confirmed that these bugs were independently rediscovered by criminals and state actors at the rate of about 20% per year. Worse, though, is that these bugs don't need to be independently rediscovered, because the NSA and CIA both leaked them. The highest-profile leak was an NSA-hoarded vulnerability in Windows they codenamed "Eternal Blue." Eternal Blue leaked in 2017, whereupon cybercriminals hybridized it with some otherwise undistinguished ransomware to create Wannacry, a devastating piece of malware that took down hospitals, banks and oil pipelines, as well as the entire city government of Baltimore and the British Library: https://cdn.sanity.io/files/v5dwkion/production/99206a2d1e9f07b35712b78f7d75fbb09560c08d.pdf But NOBUS isn't the only example of spy agencies making our computers less secure in the name of making us more secure. Perhaps the most egregious example of that are the Bundestrojaners, malicious software purchased by the German government, whose customs agents secretly installed it on the computers of unsuspecting people during border inspections. This "lawful interception" software was hugely invasive: it could grab your screen, plunder your hard drive, and install and execute software on your computer, all with the utmost stealth, intended to keep you from knowing it was installed and operating on your computer. But it wasn't merely invasive – it was insecure, so anyone (rival spies, criminals, stalkers) could scan the internet for infected computers and take them over: https://www.ccc.de/en/updates/2011/staatstrojaner You really couldn't ask for a more perfect example of the maxim that you can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure. Despite this, governments continue to demand the introduction of grave, universal secure vulnerabilities into our digital lives. Take "chat control," a proposal to force every device manufacturer to install software that continuously scans your devices for child sex abuse material (AKA "child porn"): https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/04/eu-parliament-blocks-mass-scanning-our-chats-whats-next There are plenty of things wrong with this, starting with the fact that it requires your device to secretly grab and transmit sensitive images from your phone, which might include sensitive images of your kids that were requested by their doctors. This isn't a hypothetical: it's something that happened to a dad who subsequently lost his email, his login to every other account, his phone number, all of his files (including his tax records and his business data), and every photo he had ever taken of his family, without appeal, after Google automatically detected a photo he took of his son to send to the family pediatrician. Google also falsely accused this man of sexually abusing his child and sicced the SFPD on him: https://pluralistic.net/2022/08/22/allopathic-risk/#snitches-get-stitches But even if you're not worried about this, you should still have the object permanence to recall the lessons of NOBUS and the Bundestrojaner. We can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure, and it's hard to imagine something more insecure than a computer that you entrust with every sensitive detail of your life that is designed to run computer code in secret that you can neither inspect nor terminate (let alone delete). Hardly a day goes by without some country demanding that your computer's security be weakened in the name of protecting you. For years, both Conservative and Labour UK governments have been steaming towards a total ban on working encryption in the name of catching bad guys: https://pluralistic.net/2023/03/05/theyre-still-trying-to-ban-cryptography/ It's happening in Canada, too, where somehow "digital sovereignty" means "making every device used in Canada vulnerable to foreign spies so that our own spies can access our private communications": https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/05/canadas-bill-c-22-repackaged-version-last-years-surveillance-nightmare Then there's the "age verification" laws proliferating all around the world. Remember, there's no such thing as "age verification," there's only "spying on everyone, all the time, to figure out who the kids are": https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/23/destroy-the-village/#to-save-it Age verification requires multiple entities to assemble vast corpuses of the kinds of sensitive identification papers that would allow identity thieves to destroy the finances and lives of everyone in the country, and (as foretold) every time it's tried, these files leak. Someday, this will lead to doxing whole countries: https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/02/discord-faces-backlash-over-age-checks-after-data-breach-exposed-70000-ids/ Age verification is the latest and worst stage in governments' fraught relationship with private sector data-collection. The USA is the worst offender here: it is the largest, richest country in the world that has essentially no privacy protections. The last time the US updated its federal privacy law was in 1988, when the Video Privacy Protection Act banned the disclosure of your VHS rentals. Tech companies spy on you for the same reason your dog licks its balls – because they can, and no one stops them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Which raises an obvious question: why hasn't Congress updated privacy law? And why hasn't the EU figured out how to force the US companies that pretend to be Irish to obey European privacy law? The answer is that governments love private sector data-collection, because it gives them a cheap, off-the-books source of warrantless access to information they aren't legally allowed to acquire: https://pluralistic.net/2021/04/13/public-interest-pharma/#axciom From Flock cameras to ICE's use of Google data in its ethnic cleansing campaign, the US government and the commercial surveillance industry have created a public-private partnership from hell, where governments refuse to block commercial spying and companies hand their commercial surveillance data over to governments in return. From there, it was a short leap to governments insisting that the private sector gather our data. That's the right way to think about age verification, chat control, and other mandates for corporations to spy on us using our devices and our accounts: a government requirement for private-sector mass surveillance. I have plenty of hostility to corporate overreach, but to have any hope of fighting that overreach, we need governments to be on our side. But for our governments, it comes to cybersecurity, we are the enemy, and spying corporations are our governments' allies. Sometimes, that's utterly, literally true. Governments around the world are addicted to buying spyware from cyber-arms dealers, mostly headquartered in Israel and the UAE (with the odd Italian and British company for variety). These arms-dealers practice NOBUS-by-proxy, wherein they discover or pay bounties for bugs in widely used hardware, operating systems and applications and – rather than reporting them to the manufacturer – hoard them and weaponize them, and then sell the weapons to criminals, corporations, and our governments, who give them billions of our money to ensure that our computers have huge, glaring defects in them that leave us terribly vulnerable: https://citizenlab.ca/focus-area/targeted-surveillance/ In a world where our governments' national security apparatuses were genuinely committed to our safety and security, they would criminally prosecute these companies, not make their owners into billionaires. This is the context we should all be thinking about when it comes to these "rogue AI hacking agents." The IT systems that these irresponsibly deployed software products have trashed were already terrifyingly vulnerable…by design. Rather than fix these systems, our governmental "security" agencies have spent the past 40 years making them less secure, in order to make it easier for them to catch "bad guys," who now find it trivial to attack us through systems we are all totally reliant upon. In every way, in every area of law, governments fail to take our security seriously. That even includes copyright law. All over the world, the US Trade Representative has ensured that every country has an "anti-circumvention" law that makes it a crime to reverse-engineer and modify software without permission: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition From the very start, these have been a security nightmare. Remember the "Sony Rootkit?" Between 2005-2007, Sony-BMG Music distributed over 6m CDs that were deliberately infected with a piece of malicious software called a "rootkit" that was used to disable your computer's ability to rip (copy) music CDs. The way this rootkit did so was depraved in its indifference to the security of Sony-BMG's customers: at the same time as Sony-BMG's malware installed its secret anti-ripping program, it also altered their computers' operating systems to make them incapable of detecting any program or file whose name started with $SYS$. Immediately, malicious software authors started adding $SYS$ to the start of all their filenames, and that malicious software was therefore undetectable to millions of users' computers. It was even invisible to anti-virus software. Worse: Sony-BMG's rootkit infected 200,000-300,000 US government and military networks: https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2005/11/sonys_drm_rootk.html Even worse: after the scandal broke, security researchers all over the world came forward to say that they'd discovered the Sony Rootkit months before it became common knowledge, but their lawyers had told them they weren't allowed to disclose its existence because doing so would fall afoul of anti-circumvention law. For months, this official, deliberate malware epidemic spread in secret because of anti-circumvention law. It's been more than 20 years since the Sony Rootkit, and anti-circumvention law is now worse than it was in the oughts: now it applies to far more devices from far more vendors. Today, it's common for corporations to threaten their own customers with civil and criminal liability if they have the temerity to hire outside auditors to evaluate the software they entrust their businesses to for security defects. And oh God, it's even worse, because the worst offender is Oracle, who are now the de facto IT czars of America: https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2015/08/oracle-security-chief-to-customers-stop-checking-our-code-for-vulnerabilities/ I'm not saying that these are the only problems with our IT security. What I am saying is that the hacking bots everyone's freaking out about didn't appear out of nowhere. If you have just a little object permanence, you can see that they are the terminal stage of a pathology that governments have only ever worsened: by hoarding and weaponizing vulnerabilities; by paying others to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities; by criminalizing security audits; by insisting that every computer we rely on be equipped with deliberate vulnerabilities in software we can't inspect, terminate or delete. Yeah, there should be criminal and civil liability for OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and every other company whose bots "went rogue" and attacked servers. But that will do nothing to fix our IT. The table-stakes for a secure digital world are: public agencies that try to make our computers as secure as possible, including by administering the corporate death-penalty to any company that hoards and weaponizes information about bugs in our computer. We should protect and reward individuals and firms who come forward with true disclosures about bugs in systems we rely upon. We should not give companies the right to silence and punish those critics who want to warn us about their defective products. And we should not require that companies make us less secure in the name of making it easier for spies and cops to catch the bad guys. articles.summary: The thing about Romeo and Juliet is that it is a true story. It isn't literally true, but it is literary true. We see the same motif repeated throughout all cultures and all times. Caroline Lea (writing as Caroline Finch) asks an important question - what if every pair of star-cross'd lovers were reincarnations of the original Verona duo?  The essence of tragedy is that the end is unavoidable.…

articles.title: Show HN: Guitoro, a virtual guitar you strum with your keyboard
articles.summary:
Guitoro is a free browser guitar using recordings of real instruments. You can strum with your keyboard, mouse, or touchscreen, choose acoustic, classical, electric guitar or bass, and see chord fingering and each stroke. Song practice can be slowed to 20%, and there are free chord tools and tuners. No signup or download.
1 minute video demo: https://youtu.be/DtcluMLdSgs
I would love feedback on how the strumming feels and sounds.
